findings.title: Verification walkthrough invokes a nonexistent bench entry point with nonexistent flags
findings.description:
Every command in the walkthrough uses `python scripts/bench.py --backend … --config … --N … --ticks … --subdivision-factor … --parity-check numpy`. No `scripts/bench.py` exists (`scripts/` contains only `148_measure_cell_occupancy.py` and `148_smem_vs_dram_microbench.py`), and the real CLI is `python -m migratory.bench.cli` with flags `--workload`, `--backend`, `--workload-dir`, `--results-dir` — there is no `--config`, `--N`, `--ticks`, `--subdivision-factor`, or `--parity-check` argument anywhere in `src/migratory/bench/cli.py`. The walkthrough therefore cannot be executed by an external agent as written, which defeats its purpose as the reproducibility contract. The task file for this slice inherits the same broken commands, so the defect will propagate into implementation.

The correct invocation shape is `python -m migratory.bench.cli --backend quadrants-fused --workload mid-flock-50k`, with N and tick counts coming from the workload YAML (`bench/workloads/mid-flock-50k.yaml` currently declares `n: 100000`, `warmup_ticks: 30`, `measure_ticks: 300` — note this is N=100k, not the N=50k the whole gate is specified against; the file's own description is also stale, claiming "[400,400]" while the body says `[1536.0, 1536.0]`).

findings.title: Step 3's baseline run is impossible on the branch as specified and the four-run matrix confounds the two interventions
findings.description:
Step 3 asks for four runs — "Baseline (S=1, counter-gating)", "Early exit only (S=1, break enabled)", "Cell subdivision only (S=3, counter-gating)", and "Both interventions (S=3, break enabled)" — but all four use identical flags apart from `--subdivision-factor`. There is no flag to select counter-gating vs. break; the break is permanent in the kernel. Two of the four runs are therefore literally the same command, and the other two are the same command. The design does not say how to obtain the counter-gating baseline, nor how to isolate Intervention 2's contribution.

This matters for A2/A3 attribution: the success criteria assert "≥5× faster than slice 145 CUDA baseline" and "≥100 TPS", but without a way to run the counter-gating variant on this branch, the baseline denominator must come from the recorded slice 145 number (38.3 TPS / 25.41 ms `force_total` at N=50k per `145-notes.fused-tick-measurements.md`) — which was measured at world size 756×756, not the 1536×1536 that `mid-flock-50k.yaml` currently declares. The task file (T12) explicitly says "do not attempt to re-run counter-gating on this branch (the break is permanent)" — so the design's Step 3 contradicts the task plan that implements it. Either the design should specify a runtime-selectable early-exit flag (e.g. a kernel parameter, consistent with the existing `lead_active` compile-out pattern) so the four-run matrix is real, or Step 3 should be reduced to the two runnable configurations with the baseline taken from the recorded slice 145 measurement and the workload pinned to the density-matched 756×756 world.

findings.title: Option A leaves the seam call structurally unreachable and contradicts the A7 seam-isolation invariant
findings.description:
Option A places `if k_found >= max_neighbors and max_neighbors > 0: break` **before** the `get_neighbors_first_k` call in the innermost loop. Once the cap is reached the seam is never reached again — the design says so explicitly ("The seam becomes unreachable when the break fires"). Two problems follow:

1. The break duplicates the seam's own decision logic in the kernel body. `get_neighbors_first_k` already encodes exactly this predicate (`k_max <= 0` → accept; `k_found < k_max` → accept). The existing test `tests/bench/test_quadrants_fused_kernels.py:217` (`test_get_neighbors_first_k_is_only_inclusion_function`) asserts that the selection conditional `k_found < k_max` appears **at most once** in the module and is confined to the seam. Option A's break writes `k_found >= max_neighbors` in the kernel body — semantically the same selection decision in a second place, defeating the invariant the seam exists to enforce and the invariant slice 145 A7 and slice 148 both preserved.

2. The parent's slice plan says "Both interventions use the `getNeighbors` seam already designed in slice 145 (A7)." Option A does not use the seam for the early-exit decision at all — it bypasses it. Option B (inline, remove the seam) was rejected in the design as "destroys the A7 swap point prematurely," but Option A preserves the *name* while making the function dead code on the capped path, which is a weaker form of the same loss.

The coherent alternative the design does not consider: have the seam own the decision and let the kernel act on its return value, e.g. `accept = get_neighbors_first_k(k_found, max_neighbors); if accept == 0: break` — this keeps the cap predicate in exactly one place, keeps the A7 swap point live, and still breaks out of the loop. Note the seam's `k_max <= 0` uncapped branch already returns 1 for an uncapped agent, so the `max_neighbors > 0` guard in the proposed break is redundant under that formulation.

findings.title: Cell subdivision is specified against `query_radius` but the kernel's cell size derives from `max_query_radius` across all profiles
findings.description:
The design states `cell_size = query_radius / S` and reasons about a (2S+1)×(2S+1) scan covering "the same physical radius." But `GpuAgentState.setup()` computes `self.max_query_radius = max(p.query_radius for p in profiles)` and `self.cell_size = self.max_query_radius * DEFAULT_CELL_SIZE_MULTIPLIER`. The kernel derives each agent's cell coordinates from the *global* `cell_size` parameter while filtering against that agent's *own* `query_radius` (from `profile_params`). Today every profile in `_PROFILE_REGISTRY` has `query_radius=50.0`, so the two coincide and the 3×3 scan is exactly correct.

Once `cell_size = max_query_radius / S`, a (2S+1)×(2S+1) scan covers a radius of `S * cell_size = max_query_radius` for the *largest*-radius profile — correct. But for any profile whose `query_radius` is smaller than `max_query_radius`, the scan covers more than needed (wasteful but correct), and the design never states the invariant it is relying on: **all profiles must share the same `query_radius`, or the scan extent must be derived per agent**. The document should state this precondition explicitly and note what happens if a future profile has a smaller radius. Related: with `S=3` and `query_radius=50`, `cell_size ≈ 16.7` and the scan covers ±50 units — but `query_radius`/`S` is not an integer divisor, so the (2S+1)×(2S+1) block covers `3 × 16.67 = 50.0` exactly only because S=3 and 2S+1=7 gives a half-width of 3 cells = 50.0. The design should assert the general form (half-width `S` cells × `cell_size` ≥ `query_radius`) rather than relying on the specific S=3 case.

findings.title: `BenchConfig` does not exist — the configuration integration point is misidentified
findings.description:
The Component Interactions diagram starts from `BenchConfig` with `cell_size (= query_radius / S)` and `subdivision_factor S` as its fields, and the text states "The bench harness passes `cell_size` at setup; it reads from config." No `BenchConfig` type exists anywhere in `src/migratory` (grep confirms zero hits). The actual bench configuration surface is `Workload` (`src/migratory/bench/workload.py`), a frozen dataclass whose fields are validated strictly in `from_dict` — unknown keys are silently ignored, and `n`/`dt`/`measure_ticks` are the only tuning knobs. `GpuAgentState` then derives `cell_size` itself from `max_query_radius`.

This matters because the design's config-validation story (S validated at "config-load time", before any kernel call) has no defined home under the actual architecture. The task file resolves this — T2/T3 add `subdivision_factor` to `Workload` and `GpuAgentState`, with `Workload.from_dict` doing the validation — but the design document, which is the artifact that should specify the interface, names a non-existent type and describes a config flow that does not exist. The design should name `Workload` (with `subdivision_factor: int = 1`) and `GpuAgentState` as the two config touchpoints, and state that validation lives in `Workload.from_dict` (or `GpuAgentState.setup`), with `Workload.from_dict` currently *ignoring* unrecognised YAML keys — meaning `subdivision_factor` in a YAML file would be silently dropped unless the loader is explicitly extended to read it. That silent-drop path directly contradicts the project's "never use silent fallback values" rule and is exactly the case a config-validation rule needs to cover.

findings.title: NFR restatement does not cover the N=100k+ regime the slice's own premises push toward
findings.description: The slice restates the Tier 2 NFR (60 TPS at N=50k on CUDA) and gates above it, which satisfies the NFR-restatement requirement for the operating point it targets. But the premise comes from slice 148's envelope measurements, which show the working set spills from L2 to DRAM between N=50k and N=100k, and the parent plan places Tier 3 at 250k. The early-exit intervention reduces *work*, not *bytes*, so it may not help in the bandwidth-bound regime at all — and indeed slice 148's notes recorded that density-independence at N=50k initially pointed to a memory-bound (not work-bound) kernel, which the later occupancy analysis refuted. The slice does not restate any NFR for N≥100k and does not state whether the intervention is expected to help there. The parent's Tier 3 milestone (250k) and the architecture's memory-budget table go unaddressed, so the slice cannot be judged against the tier it is a prerequisite for. A brief statement of the expected behavior at N=100k/250k — even if it is "expected to be neutral, measurement deferred to the Tier 3 validation slice" — is needed.

findings.title: Warp-divergence analysis assumes spatial adjacency that the agent ordering does not provide
findings.description:
The divergence argument rests on "threads in the same warp (agents with similar spatial index) hit the cap within a small, similar iteration window." In `fused_force_integrate_kernel` the parallel loop is `for i in range(n)` over agent index `i`, and the parallel `range_for` maps consecutive `i` to consecutive lanes — so warp lanes are consecutive *agent indices*, not spatially adjacent agents. Agents are shuffled by `rng.shuffle(profile_indices)` at setup and placed round-robin into two flocks, so consecutive agent indices are scattered across the two clusters and across cells. Spatial adjacency is only recovered *inside* the kernel via `sorted_agent_ids`, which orders candidates within a cell — but that reordering happens after the per-lane divergence has already been determined by where each lane's own first-32-neighbors sit in the candidate stream.

The practical effect is that lanes within a warp will generally hit the cap at *different* iteration counts, which is the divergence-expensive case, not the favourable one. The design's conclusion (wasted-work saving dominates) is likely still right — the saving is ~45,000 iterations versus a divergence penalty bounded by warp width — but the stated mechanism is wrong, and the design gives no measurement plan for divergence. Since A2's 5× and A3's 100 TPS are both generous relative to the ~50/45,000 = 0.1% theoretical iteration reduction, the risk is low; still, the divergence reasoning should be corrected rather than left asserting an adjacency property the code does not have.

findings.title: A5's verification method is not reproducible on the CUDA host
findings.description:
A5 requires "local memory per thread = 0 (confirmed via `nvcc --ptxas-info` or benchmark log)" but Step 4 says to "look for `lmem` in the bench log output (Quadrants/Taichi emits ptxas info when `TI_PRINT_KERNEL_STATS=1` or equivalent)". The 148 envelope notes record that on this exact CUDA host "`ptxas`, `cuobjdump`, and `nvcc` are not installed — only the CUDA runtime driver," and that the working method was PTX inspection of the Quadrants kernel cache at `~/.cache/quadrants/qdcache/ptx_cache_sm_86/…ptx`, checking for `.local` declarations (the hot kernel `…_kernel_1_range_for` showed `.local` = 0). `TI_PRINT_KERNEL_STATS` is a Taichi env var name; Quadrants is a Taichi fork, but nothing in the repo or the notes confirms that flag emits `lmem` for this backend.

Step 4 should name the method that is known to work on this host: inspect the cached PTX for the fused kernel and assert zero `.local` declarations. The task file's T13 has the same gap.

findings.title: S upper bound of 8 is asserted against a cell-count heuristic that does not match the actual grid arithmetic
findings.description:
The rationale for capping S at 8 is that "S=8 gives a 17×17 = 289-cell scan, which is already larger than the physical neighborhood … and risks pushing `grid_w * grid_h * cell_count` auxiliary arrays past practical GPU memory." But the grid does not grow with the *scan* extent — `grid_w`/`grid_h` grow with S² because `cell_size` shrinks. At N=50k with `query_radius=50` and S=8, `cell_size=6.25` and a 1536×1536 world gives a 246×246 grid = ~60,000 cells, well under `MAX_CELLS_SANITY_CAP = 4_000_000` in `quadrants_fused_state.py`. The real cost driver at high S is (a) the per-agent (2S+1)² cell-visit loop — 289 cell lookups per agent instead of 9 — and (b) the CPU prefix sum over `n_cells`, which grows as S².

The bound is still defensible as a conservative guard, but the stated reasoning is wrong on the memory point (the arrays do not approach GPU-memory limits at S=8 for realistic workloads) and does not mention the dominant cost, which is the per-agent cell-visit count. Stating the correct driver would also make the S=3 default (49 cell visits per agent vs. 9) legible as the actual tradeoff.

findings.title: `S=3` scan does not reduce candidate count by S² as claimed, and the interaction analysis understates the gain
findings.description:
The document asserts "Agents/cell drops from ~5000 to ~5000/S² ≈ 555" and that "the scan covers the same physical radius — correct neighborhood is preserved." Both are correct per-cell, but the scan now visits (2S+1)² = 49 cells instead of 9, so total candidates scanned per agent is roughly 49 × 555 ≈ 27,000 versus 9 × 5,000 = 45,000 — a ~1.7× reduction, not S². The slice 148 re-diagnosis notes state this correctly ("49 cells × 555 = ~27,000 candidates — still better than 45,000"), so the design has lost precision relative to its own source.

This is not merely cosmetic: it changes the expected contribution of Intervention 2, which is the entire justification for carrying S as a configurable knob. If Intervention 2 buys only ~1.7× and Intervention 1 buys ~1400× in iteration count, then S is a second-order knob whose own cost (49 vs. 9 cell-visit iterations per agent, plus a 9× larger grid and prefix sum) could plausibly exceed its benefit once early exit is in place. The design should either state that S=3 is retained primarily as a warp-divergence/load-balancing lever and cite the measurement that justifies it, or mark it as an experiment whose value is unproven at the gate configuration.
